questions.question: How do application.properties, application.yml, and environment variables differ in Spring Boot configuration?
questions.title: application.properties vs application.yml vs Environment Variables
questions.direct_answer: Spring Boot loads configuration from many sources and merges them into a unified `Environment` with a strict precedence order: **command-line args > environment variables > profile-specific files > base `application.{yml,properties}` > defaults**. `application.yml` supports hierarchical structure and multi-document files; `application.properties` is flat key=value pairs — both have the same precedence, so the file loaded last wins for duplicates. Environment variables use **relaxed binding** (`SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL` maps to `spring.datasource.url`) and are essential for twelve-factor app deployments where credentials and per-environment values must be injected at runtime, never committed to source.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate knows precedence rules and can decide which mechanism to use in a given environment (local dev vs CI vs production Kubernetes)
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Assuming `application.yml` always wins over `application.properties` — in fact they have the same precedence, and if both exist Spring Boot loads both with properties processed first, so yml values win for duplicates
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention profile-specific files (`application-prod.yml`), Spring Cloud Config Server, and the full PropertySource order documented in Spring Boot reference docs

sections.title: The Property Source Stack That Most Developers Get Wrong
sections.content:
The most common misconception is that `application.yml` overrides `application.properties` (or vice versa). **They have identical precedence** — if both exist with the same property, the one loaded last wins. This is a trick question in interviews, and most candidates get it wrong.

What actually matters is Spring Boot's **layered property source ordering**.
- Command-line arguments override environment variables, which override `application-{profile}.{yml,properties}`, which override `application.{yml,properties}`, which override `@PropertySource` annotations, which override defaults.
- The hierarchy goes from most specific (command line) to least specific (code defaults), and **the first value found wins** — Spring doesn't merge values across levels.

This design solves a real deployment problem: write defaults in `application.yml`, override per environment with `application-prod.yml`, override individual values at deploy time with environment variables (which play well with Docker and Kubernetes), and force values during debugging with command-line arguments. **Each layer exists for a reason**, and understanding the order prevents the most common production configuration bug — a value that works locally but gets silently overridden in deployment.

sections.title: Properties vs YAML vs Environment Variables — Format, Strength, and When Each Wins
sections.content:
The choice between formats isn't just syntax preference — each has genuine trade-offs that affect readability, tooling, and deployment.

| Aspect | application.properties | application.yml | Environment Variables |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Syntax** | Flat key=value pairs | Hierarchical YAML with indentation | `SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL` (uppercase, underscores) |
| **Precedence** | Same level as .yml | Same level as .properties | Higher — overrides both file types |
| **Multi-document** | Not supported | `---` separates profile sections in one file | N/A |
| **Type safety** | Strings only, no native lists | Lists, maps, nested objects natively | Strings only |
| **Tooling** | IDE autocomplete works well | Indentation errors cause silent failures | Platform-dependent (Docker, K8s) |
| **Secrets** | Visible in source control | Visible in source control | Injected at runtime, not in code |
| **Profile-specific** | `application-prod.properties` | `application-prod.yml` or multi-document | `SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=prod` |

**The practical recommendation:** use YAML for readable, hierarchical config in source control. Use environment variables for anything that changes per deployment — database URLs, API keys, feature flags. Never commit secrets in either file format. The combination of YAML defaults plus environment variable overrides is the pattern most production teams settle on.

sections.title: Profile-Specific Files and the External Config Pattern
sections.content:
**Profile-specific loading**
- If `spring.profiles.active=prod`, then `application-prod.yml` is loaded automatically
- Its values override the base `application.yml` for any keys that overlap
- Multiple active profiles are merged in order: `application-prod.yml` then `application-prod-eu.yml`

**Multi-document YAML for inline profiles**
- A single `application.yml` can contain multiple documents separated by `---`
- Each document can target a profile via `spring.config.activate.on-profile`

```yaml
spring:
  application:
    name: order-service
server:
  port: 8080
---
spring:
  config:
    activate.on-profile: prod
server:
  port: 80
  forward-headers-strategy: native
```

**External config directory**
- Spring Boot looks for `config/` next to the JAR before checking inside the JAR
- An ops team can drop `config/application-prod.yml` next to the JAR without rebuilding
- The lookup order: `./config/`, `./`, `classpath:/config/`, `classpath:/`

**Spring Cloud Config Server**
- Centralizes configuration across all services and serves values over HTTP
- Supports versioning through Git and runtime refresh via `@RefreshScope`
- Plugged in with `spring.config.import=configserver:http://config-server:8888` in `application.yml`

sections.title: Verify Loaded Values via /actuator/env
sections.content:
**Why the env endpoint matters**
- A misindented YAML property silently becomes part of the wrong key — you get the default value instead of your configured one
- The `/actuator/env` endpoint shows every PropertySource in priority order with the resolved value

**Enable and inspect**

```properties
management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=env,configprops,health
management.endpoint.env.show-values=when-authorized
```

**Sample response excerpt**

```json
{
  "propertySources": [
    { "name": "commandLineArgs", "properties": { "server.port": { "value": "9090" } } },
    { "name": "systemEnvironment", "properties": { "server.port": { "value": "8080", "origin": "env var" } } },
    { "name": "applicationConfig: [classpath:/application.yml]",
      "properties": { "server.port": { "value": "8080" } } }
  ]
}
```

**Operational notes**
- The `--debug` startup flag also prints the conditions evaluation report which lists active property sources
- `/actuator/configprops` shows resolved `@ConfigurationProperties` beans with their bound values
- `show-values=when-authorized` is the production setting — `always` leaks credentials

sections.title: Configuration Source Trade-offs
sections.content:
**When YAML helps:**
- Hierarchical config with nested objects, lists, and maps
- Multiple profile sections in one file via `---`
- Type-rich values like durations and data sizes

**When YAML hurts:**
- Indentation typos cause silent failures — a misindented key becomes part of the wrong section
- `key:` (null) and `key: ""` (empty string) behave differently; `@Value("${key}")` on a null YAML property throws `IllegalArgumentException`
- Parsing is sensitive to tabs vs spaces — many editors are unforgiving

**When properties files help:**
- Flat key-value pairs with no indentation surprises
- IDE autocomplete and refactoring tend to be slightly more reliable
- Easier to grep and diff in version control

**When environment variables help:**
- Twelve-factor compliance — config changes per deploy without rebuilding
- Container orchestrators (Kubernetes, ECS) inject secrets via env
- Relaxed binding handles the case differences automatically

**Watch for:**
- Same property in multiple sources — only the highest-precedence value applies; other values are silently shadowed
- Lists in env vars use indexed names: `MY_LIST_0=a`, `MY_LIST_1=b` to bind a `List<String>`
- Setting `spring.profiles.active` in `application.yml` is brittle — prefer the env var or `--spring.profiles.active`

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Properties and YAML at the same level have equal priority** — if both `application.properties` and `application.yml` exist, properties is loaded first and yml second; the file loaded last wins for any key in both.
- **Environment variables beat property files** — Spring Boot's external configuration priority: command-line args > env vars > profile-specific properties > `application.{yml,properties}`.
- **YAML null vs empty string** — `key:` (null) and `key: ""` (empty string) behave differently; `@Value("${key}")` on a null YAML property throws `IllegalArgumentException`.
- **Relaxed binding for env vars** — `SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL` maps to `spring.datasource.url`; underscores replace dots and dashes; Spring Boot handles this automatically.
- **`spring.config.import` for external files** — import additional config from file system, classpath, or config servers: `spring.config.import=file:/etc/app/secrets.properties`.
- **`/actuator/env` is the source of truth** — when a value isn't behaving as expected, the endpoint shows every property source and which one resolved the value.
- **Profile-specific files override base files** — `application-prod.yml` automatically applied when `spring.profiles.active=prod`.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Spring Boot aggregates configuration from multiple sources with a strict priority order. Knowing the order is essential for understanding why a property has a particular value in a given environment.

**Priority order (highest to lowest)**
- Command-line arguments (`--server.port=9090`) — always win
- Environment variables (`SERVER_PORT=9090`) — override property files; the standard for Docker and Kubernetes
- Profile-specific files (`application-prod.properties`) — override the base file for active profiles
- `application.properties` / `application.yml` — the base defaults

**Properties vs YAML**
- `application.properties`: flat key-value, readable, no indentation sensitivity
- `application.yml`: hierarchical structure, good for deeply nested config; but YAML null vs empty string behavior is a common trap — `key:` is null, which causes `@Value("${key}")` to throw `IllegalArgumentException`
- If both files exist at the same location, properties is loaded first; yml takes precedence for any key in both

**Environment variable relaxed binding**
- `SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL` automatically maps to `spring.datasource.url` — dots and dashes become underscores; uppercase is standard for container environments

**Verifying configuration**
- `/actuator/env` shows every property source in priority order so you can see exactly which value was resolved
- `--debug` prints the conditions evaluation report for auto-configuration

Use property files for developer defaults, profile-specific files for environment overrides, and environment variables or secrets managers for production credentials — never hardcode credentials in any property file committed to version control.

questions.question: When should you use @ConfigurationProperties instead of @Value in Spring Boot?
questions.title: @ConfigurationProperties vs @Value
questions.direct_answer: `@Value` injects a single property value using SpEL and is convenient for one-off values, but it has **no validation, no relaxed binding, no IDE autocompletion**, and no support for nested types. `@ConfigurationProperties` binds an entire **prefix of related properties** to a typed POJO, supports JSR-303 Bean Validation, relaxed binding (camelCase, kebab-case, UPPER_SNAKE_CASE), constructor binding for immutability, and generates IDE metadata. The rule: `@Value` for one or two isolated values; `@ConfigurationProperties` for any group sharing a prefix.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate knows the practical limitations of `@Value` and can justify when the more verbose `@ConfigurationProperties` approach is worth it
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using `@Value` for every property, even large groups of related config, resulting in classes littered with `@Value` fields and no validation
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that `@ConfigurationProperties` requires `@EnableConfigurationProperties` or `@ConfigurationPropertiesScan`, supports constructor binding via Java records, and that `spring-boot-configuration-processor` generates IDE metadata

sections.title: Why @Value Breaks Down at Scale
sections.content:
In small applications with three or four properties, `@Value("${some.prop}")` works fine.
- The problem appears when you have **20+ related configuration values** — database pool settings, retry policies, feature flags — scattered across multiple beans.
- Each `@Value` field is a raw string injection with **no type safety, no validation, no IDE support** for refactoring.
- Rename a property key in `application.yml` and nothing fails at compile time — you get a runtime `IllegalArgumentException` or worse, a silent null.

`@ConfigurationProperties` solves this by **binding an entire prefix of your configuration to a typed Java object**.
- Instead of twenty `@Value` annotations, you get a single POJO with fields that match the property keys.
- Spring Boot's relaxed binding handles `camelCase`, `kebab-case`, and `UPPER_SNAKE_CASE` automatically.
- You get IDE autocomplete for your custom properties through `spring-boot-configuration-processor`, JSR-303 validation with `@Validated`, and immutable configuration using constructor binding.

The trade-off is **setup overhead**. `@ConfigurationProperties` requires either `@EnableConfigurationProperties(MyProps.class)` on a configuration class or `@ConfigurationPropertiesScan` on the main class.
- For a single property, that's unnecessary ceremony.
- The dividing line is clear: **one or two isolated properties → `@Value`; a group of related properties → `@ConfigurationProperties`.**

sections.title: @Value vs @ConfigurationProperties — What Each Actually Gives You
sections.content:
The differences go beyond syntax — they affect testability, safety, and how configuration evolves as the application grows.

| Aspect | @Value | @ConfigurationProperties |
|---|---|---|
| **Binding** | Single property per annotation | Entire prefix mapped to a POJO |
| **Type safety** | String by default, manual conversion | Automatic type conversion + nested objects |
| **Validation** | No built-in validation | `@Validated` with JSR-303 annotations (`@NotNull`, `@Min`) |
| **IDE support** | No autocomplete for custom props | `spring-boot-configuration-processor` generates metadata |
| **Immutability** | Mutable fields only | Constructor binding with `@ConstructorBinding` (pre-3.x) or record classes |
| **SpEL support** | Full SpEL: `#{T(Math).random()}` | No SpEL — pure property binding |
| **Refactoring** | Rename breaks silently at runtime | Type-safe, caught at startup |
| **Testing** | Inject via `@TestPropertySource` | Instantiate POJO directly in unit tests |

**The SpEL point is the exception where `@Value` wins.** If you need a computed default like `@Value("#{${retry.max:3} * 2}")`, `@ConfigurationProperties` can't do that. But SpEL in configuration is a code smell in most cases — prefer computing values in code.

sections.title: Constructor Binding with Java Records
IDE Metadata via the Annotation Processor
sections.content:
**Add the processor**
- The `spring-boot-configuration-processor` generates `META-INF/spring-configuration-metadata.json` at compile time
- Without it, custom properties show as warnings in the IDE: "unknown property"

**Maven setup**

```xml
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-configuration-processor</artifactId>
    <optional>true</optional>
</dependency>
```

**Gradle setup**

```groovy
annotationProcessor 'org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-configuration-processor'
```

**What the processor produces**
- A JSON file describing every property name, type, default value, and Javadoc description
- IDEs (IntelliJ, VS Code, Eclipse) read this metadata to provide autocomplete in `application.yml` and `application.properties`
- The processor extracts Javadoc from your record components or POJO fields as documentation tooltips

**Adding manual hints**

```javadoc
/**
 * Maximum HikariCP pool size.
 * @param maxPoolSize positive integer; values above 50 require platform team approval
 */
```

- Custom enums and limited value sets can be declared in `additional-spring-configuration-metadata.json` for richer IDE support

sections.title: @Value vs @ConfigurationProperties Trade-offs
sections.content:
**When @Value helps:**
- Single isolated property where activating `@ConfigurationProperties` is overkill
- Computed defaults using SpEL: `@Value("#{environment.acceptsProfiles('prod') ? 100 : 10}")`
- Quick prototypes where setup overhead matters more than safety

**When @Value hurts:**
- More than 3 related properties — refactoring becomes painful
- Need for validation — there's no built-in mechanism
- Need for nested objects, lists, or maps — SpEL workarounds get ugly fast
- Tests require Spring context just to inject a value

**When @ConfigurationProperties helps:**
- Groups of related properties under a common prefix
- Type-safe configuration with compile-time refactoring safety
- JSR-303 validation that fails fast at startup
- Immutable config via records or constructor binding

**Watch for:**
- `@ConfigurationProperties` class without `@Component`, `@EnableConfigurationProperties`, or `@ConfigurationPropertiesScan` — silently never populated
- Validation runs at startup only — values changed via `/actuator/refresh` are not re-validated unless `@Validated` is wired through `@RefreshScope`
- Record components don't support `@Validated` cascading into nested records without explicit `@Valid`

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`@ConfigurationProperties` requires `@EnableConfigurationProperties` or `@ConfigurationPropertiesScan`** — or the class must be annotated with `@Component`; without one of these, the POJO is never populated.
- **`@ConfigurationProperties` validates at startup; `@Value` validates at first use** — `@Validated` + JSR-303 annotations on a `@ConfigurationProperties` class fail startup with a clear message listing every missing required field.
- **`@ConfigurationProperties` auto-converts `Duration`, `DataSize`, and `List`** — `timeout: 30s` binds to a `Duration` field automatically; `@Value` requires manual parsing.
- **`@Value` for one-off values; `@ConfigurationProperties` for anything with a prefix** — three related properties sharing a prefix = migrate to `@ConfigurationProperties`.
- **`spring-boot-configuration-processor` generates IDE metadata** — add as an annotation processor; your custom properties get auto-completion and documentation in IDEs.
- **Java records make constructor binding trivial** — immutable, validated, scannable, no boilerplate.
- **`@RefreshScope` + Spring Cloud** — combined with `@ConfigurationProperties`, properties can be refreshed at runtime via `/actuator/refresh`.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
`@Value` and `@ConfigurationProperties` both inject external configuration, but they are designed for different scales. Choosing the wrong one creates code that is hard to test, hard to validate, and hard for teammates to discover.

**`@Value` — for isolated one-off values**
- `@Value("${api.key}")` injects a single property; works fine for one or two standalone values
- No validation at startup — a missing required property causes an NPE at the first call site, not at startup
- No type conversion for structured types — `Duration`, `DataSize`, `List` require manual parsing

**`@ConfigurationProperties` — for groups of related properties**
- Binds an entire prefix to a POJO: `@ConfigurationProperties(prefix = "payment")` maps `payment.url`, `payment.timeout`, `payment.retries` to fields automatically
- Add `@Validated` and JSR-303 annotations — missing required fields cause a clear startup failure with every violation listed
- Auto-converts `Duration` (`30s`), `DataSize` (`256MB`), `List` (comma-separated strings)
- Generates IDE auto-completion metadata when `spring-boot-configuration-processor` is added as an annotation processor

**Activation**
- The class needs either `@Component`, `@EnableConfigurationProperties(MyConfig.class)` in a `@Configuration` class, or `@ConfigurationPropertiesScan` on the main class

The rule: `@Value` for a single isolated key, `@ConfigurationProperties` for anything that has a prefix and more than two properties.

questions.question: How do you configure logging in Spring Boot — log levels, Logback, and structured logging?
questions.title: Spring Boot Logging — Logback Configuration, Log Levels, and Structured Logs
questions.direct_answer: Spring Boot uses **Logback by default** with sensible console output. Log levels are set via `logging.level.*` properties per package — `logging.level.root=WARN` plus `logging.level.com.example=DEBUG` is the typical pattern. For production, **structured JSON logging** through `logback-spring.xml` with the Logstash encoder enables log aggregation in ELK, Loki, and Splunk. Spring profiles (`<springProfile>` blocks) control which configuration applies per environment. Use `logback-spring.xml` (not `logback.xml`) so Spring Boot manages loading and profile support is available.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate can configure logging beyond the defaults and understands per-package log levels
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using `logback.xml` instead of `logback-spring.xml`, losing Spring profile support and property placeholders in the logging config
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention structured JSON logging with Logstash encoder for production, MDC for correlation IDs, and the requirement to clear MDC in a `finally` block to avoid leaking context across pooled threads

sections.title: logback.xml vs logback-spring.xml — The Filename That Breaks Profile Support
sections.content:
The most common logging mistake in Spring Boot isn't the format or the level — it's the filename. **Using `logback.xml` instead of `logback-spring.xml`** means you lose Spring profile-aware configuration and property placeholder support. `logback.xml` is loaded by Logback directly, before Spring's environment is ready. `logback-spring.xml` is loaded by Spring Boot, giving you access to `<springProfile>` blocks and `${spring.application.name}` placeholders.

Boot's default logging is sensible for development: **console output with timestamp, level, logger name, and message**. But production needs differ — you want JSON-structured output for log aggregation tools (ELK, Splunk, Datadog), per-package log levels to reduce noise, and file rotation to prevent disk exhaustion.

**Log levels cascade from root downward**.
- Setting `logging.level.root=WARN` quiets everything, then `logging.level.com.example=DEBUG` enables verbose logging only for your code.
- This granularity means you can debug your application without drowning in Spring framework or Hibernate noise.
- For production, the **structured JSON + MDC correlation ID** combination is what makes logs operationally useful at scale.

sections.title: Setting Log Levels via Properties
sections.content:
**Property-based level overrides**
- `logging.level.root=WARN` — silence everything by default
- `logging.level.com.example=DEBUG` — verbose for your packages only
- `logging.level.org.hibernate.SQL=DEBUG` — log SQL statements for query debugging
- `logging.level.org.hibernate.type.descriptor.sql.BasicBinder=TRACE` — log bind parameters too

**application.yml**

```yaml
logging:
  level:
    root: WARN
    com.example.orders: DEBUG
    org.springframework.web: INFO
  pattern:
    console: "%d{HH:mm:ss.SSS} [%thread] %-5level %logger{36} - %msg%n"
  file:
    name: /var/log/app/application.log
  logback:
    rollingpolicy:
      max-file-size: 100MB
      max-history: 30
```

**Profile-specific levels**
- `application-dev.yml` — DEBUG for your packages, full SQL logging
- `application-prod.yml` — WARN for root, INFO for your packages, no SQL logging

**Runtime level changes via Actuator**
- Enable `loggers` endpoint: `management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=loggers`
- POST to `/actuator/loggers/com.example` with `{"configuredLevel":"DEBUG"}` to flip levels without redeploy
- Always protect this endpoint with role-based auth — runtime DEBUG can flood logs

sections.title: Structured JSON Logging for Production
sections.content:
**Why structured JSON**
- Log aggregation tools (Elasticsearch, Loki, CloudWatch) parse JSON natively
- Each event is a single JSON object — no multi-line stack trace association problems
- Custom fields (correlation ID, user ID, service name) become first-class searchable attributes

**Add the Logstash encoder**

```xml
<dependency>
    <groupId>net.logstash.logback</groupId>
    <artifactId>logstash-logback-encoder</artifactId>
    <version>7.4</version>
</dependency>
```

**logback-spring.xml with profile-aware appenders**

```xml
<configuration>
    <springProfile name="prod">
        <appender name="STDOUT" class="ch.qos.logback.core.ConsoleAppender">
            <encoder class="net.logstash.logback.encoder.LogstashEncoder">
                <includeMdcKeyName>correlationId</includeMdcKeyName>
                <includeMdcKeyName>userId</includeMdcKeyName>
                <customFields>{"service":"order-service"}</customFields>
            </encoder>
        </appender>
    </springProfile>

    <springProfile name="dev">
        <appender name="STDOUT" class="ch.qos.logback.core.ConsoleAppender">
            <encoder>
                <pattern>%d{HH:mm:ss} [%X{correlationId}] %-5level %logger{36} - %msg%n</pattern>
            </encoder>
        </appender>
    </springProfile>

    <root level="INFO">
        <appender-ref ref="STDOUT"/>
    </root>
</configuration>
```

**Production logging in containers**
- Always log to `stdout` — Kubernetes and Docker collect stdout/stderr for log aggregation
- Never log to a file inside the container — pod restart loses the logs
- Avoid `RollingFileAppender` in containers; let the platform handle rotation

sections.title: MDC for Request Tracing
Logging Configuration Trade-offs
sections.content:
**When structured JSON helps:**
- Centralized log aggregation in Elasticsearch, Loki, CloudWatch, Splunk
- Multi-service deployments where you query across services by correlation ID
- High log volume where text parsing is too expensive at index time

**When structured JSON hurts:**
- Local development — JSON is harder to read by eye than a formatted pattern
- Single-service deployments without centralized aggregation
- Constrained environments where the encoder dependency adds notable startup time

**Watch for:**
- `logback.xml` instead of `logback-spring.xml` — silently disables `<springProfile>` and `<springProperty>`
- Stale MDC values from missing `MDC.clear()` in a `finally` block
- Logging credentials, tokens, or PII at any level — search for `password`, `token`, `email` in your codebase before shipping
- Excessive DEBUG in production — bursting log volume can fill disks and overwhelm aggregation pipelines
- Synchronous appenders blocking request threads — wrap with `AsyncAppender` for high-throughput services

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Use `logback-spring.xml`, not `logback.xml`** — `logback-spring.xml` gives Spring Boot control; you can use `<springProfile name="prod">` blocks for profile-based config; `logback.xml` is loaded before Spring Boot initializes.
- **`logging.level.com.example=DEBUG` overrides logback config** — Spring Boot's property-based logging configuration applies on top of the XML config; useful for temporary debugging without redeployment.
- **Log to `stdout`, not to a file, in containers** — Docker and Kubernetes collect `stdout`/`stderr` and forward to the log aggregation platform; writing to a file inside the container loses logs when the pod restarts.
- **Structured JSON logging for production** — add `logstash-logback-encoder` and configure a `LogstashEncoder`; each log line is a JSON object parseable by Elasticsearch, Loki, and CloudWatch Logs.
- **MDC for distributed tracing** — `MDC.put("correlationId", id)` adds fields to every log line in the current thread; always clear in a `finally` block to avoid stale values on pooled threads.
- **`/actuator/loggers` for runtime level changes** — POST to flip a package to DEBUG without redeploying; protect with role-based auth.
- **`AsyncAppender` for high-throughput** — wrap blocking appenders so logging doesn't slow request threads.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Spring Boot uses Logback by default and configures it with sensible defaults — console output at INFO level, pattern-based formatting. Production applications need more: profile-specific levels, structured JSON output, and correlation IDs.

**`logback-spring.xml` over `logback.xml`**
- `logback-spring.xml` loads through Spring Boot's logging system — you get `<springProfile name="prod">` blocks that activate by active profile, and `<springProperty>` to read from `application.properties`
- `logback.xml` is loaded by Logback directly before Spring initializes — no profile support, no property access

**Property overrides**
- `logging.level.com.example=DEBUG` in `application.properties` adds debug logging for your packages without touching XML
- Combine with profiles: `application-dev.yml` sets DEBUG; `application-prod.yml` sets WARN

**Production patterns**
- Log to stdout in containers — Kubernetes collects it and forwards to your log aggregation system; file logs are lost when pods restart
- Use `logstash-logback-encoder` for JSON output — one JSON object per line, parseable by Elasticsearch and Loki without custom regex
- Add MDC fields for distributed tracing: `traceId`, `spanId`, `userId` on every log line allow filtering across services
- Always clear MDC in a `finally` block — pooled threads carry stale values otherwise

**Runtime debugging**
- `/actuator/loggers` POST flips a package to DEBUG without redeploying — protect with auth
- `AsyncAppender` keeps logging off the critical request path for high-throughput services
